title: Siegel Zeros: Can L(1, χ) Be Very Small? (Open Question)
description: Can L(1, χ) be extremely close to zero for real Dirichlet characters χ of large conductor? Dirichlet's theorem (in Mathlib) proves L(1, χ) ≠ 0, but how small can it get? A 'Siegel zero' would be a real zero β of L(s, χ) in (1 - c/log(q), 1) — their existence is a major open question in analytic number theory, intimately connected to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

meta.author: Open (Siegel 1935 for bounds; Landau-Page theorem; Goldfeld 1976 conditional on GRH)

overview.historicalContext:
Dirichlet's 1837 theorem that L(1, χ) ≠ 0 for non-trivial characters was the key analytic step for proving infinitely many primes in arithmetic progressions. But knowing L(1, χ) is nonzero doesn't tell us HOW SMALL it can be. This quantitative question turned out to be extraordinarily deep.

In 1935, Siegel proved (ineffectively!) that L(1, χ) > C(ε)/q^ε for any fixed ε > 0, where C(ε) is a positive constant. The catch: the proof of C(ε) > 0 is non-constructive (it uses a 'Siegel zero repulsion' argument). No one has ever been able to make it effective.

The term 'Siegel zero' refers to a hypothetical real zero of L(s, χ) very close to s = 1. If such a zero β exists with β > 1 - c/log(q), then by the mean value theorem L(1, χ) ~ (1-β) is exponentially small, contradicting what's needed for primes in progressions.

The Landau-Page theorem (proved by Landau in 1918 and Page in 1935) shows at most ONE primitive real character per conductor range can have a Siegel zero. This 'exceptional character' phenomenon is the heart of the open question.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question (dirichlets-theorem-oq-01)**: Do Siegel zeros exist? That is, does there exist a sequence of real primitive Dirichlet characters χ_q of conductor q → ∞ with a real zero β_q of L(s, χ_q) satisfying β_q > 1 - c/log(q)?

**Equivalently**: Is Siegel's lower bound L(1, χ) > C(ε)/q^ε sharp (up to the ε), or can we prove an effective lower bound L(1, χ) ≫ 1/log(q)?

**What IS known**:
- L(1, χ) ≠ 0 for all non-trivial χ (Mathlib, proved)
- L(1, χ) > C(ε)/q^ε for any ε > 0 (Siegel 1935, proved but ineffective)
- At most one exceptional character per conductor range (Landau-Page, proved)
- Conditional on GRH: L(1, χ) ≫ 1/(log q)² (effective, GRH → no Siegel zeros)
- Siegel zeros: **OPEN** (expected impossible, but unproved).

overview.proofStrategy:
We formalize the current state of knowledge:

**1. Nonvanishing (proved)**: `L_one_ne_zero` wraps Mathlib's `LFunction_apply_one_ne_zero`, which is the key step in Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.

**2. Definitions**: `IsSiegelZero`, `HasSiegelZero`, `SiegelZeroConjecture` formalize the geometric picture: a Siegel zero is a real zero in the 'forbidden region' (1 - c/log(q), 1).

**3. Key implication (proved)**: `siegel_zero_implies_small_L_one` shows that a Siegel zero β implies |L(1,χ)| ≤ (1-β)·M for some derivative bound M. The proof is complete (no sorry): it takes a derivative bound on [β,1] as a hypothesis and discharges the Mean Value Theorem calculation via `differentiable_LFunction`, `HasDerivAt.comp_ofReal`, and `norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_deriv_le_segment'`.

**4. Partial results (axiomized)**:
- `siegel_theorem`: The ineffective lower bound L(1,χ) > C(ε)/q^ε (requires Landau-Page machinery not in Mathlib)
- `grh_implies_no_siegel_zeros`: GRH implies the effective bound ≫ 1/(log q)² (requires GRH itself)
- `landau_page_theorem`: At most one exceptional character per range (requires deep zero-free region theory)

**5. Consequences**: `siegel_zero_location_constraint` chains the Siegel axiom to give concrete lower bounds on L(1,χ) regardless of zero locations.
keyInsights: The key difficulty: Siegel's proof of C(ε) > 0 uses a 'self-referential' argument — it considers two hypothetical near-Siegel-zero characters and shows they repel each other, forcing at most one to exist. This non-constructive trick is why the constant C(ε) cannot be made effective
GRH (no zeros with Re(s) > 1/2) immediately implies no Siegel zeros, since Siegel zeros have β → 1 which is > 1/2. So GRH solves this problem as a special case

Siegel zeros would have dramatic consequences: they are intimately connected to Chebyshev's bias, the distribution of primes in progressions, and Linnik's theorem on the smallest prime in an arithmetic progression

The Landau-Page theorem gives a useful structure: among all real primitive characters of conductor ≤ Q, AT MOST ONE can have a Siegel zero. This 'exceptional character' monopolizes the potential zeros
Mathlib's `LFunction_apply_one_ne_zero` gives L(1,χ) ≠ 0 for free — the Siegel zero question is purely quantitative, asking how close to 0 is possible
prerequisites: Number theory (arithmetic progressions, primes in residue classes)

sections.mathContext: Siegel (1935): $L(1,\chi) \gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ (ineffective); GRH eliminates Siegel zeros.

sections.title: Part V: The Landau-Page Theorem
sections.summary: Axiomatizes `landau_page_theorem`: at most one exceptional (Siegel-zero-bearing) character per conductor range.

sections.mathContext: Formalizes the open question of whether an exact Siegel zero can occur, given L(1,χ)≠0.

sections.title: Part VII: Structural Properties of Siegel Zeros

sections.mathContext: Constraints on a Siegel zero's location ($0<\beta<1$, near 1) and GRH-based elimination results.

sections.title: Part VIII: Additional Structural Results

sections.title: Part IX: Deuring-Heilbronn Zero Repulsion
sections.summary: Axiomatizes `deuring_heilbronn_repulsion` (a Siegel zero repels all other zeros of L-functions) and derives `siegel_zero_repels_other_zeros` and `repulsion_grows_with_proximity`.
sections.mathContext: Deuring-Heilbronn phenomenon: a Siegel zero pushes other zeros away, more strongly the closer it is to 1.

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures the current state of knowledge about Siegel zeros. While L(1,χ) ≠ 0 is fully proved in Mathlib, whether it can be exponentially small remains open. We formalize: (1) the nonvanishing result, (2) the definition of Siegel zeros, (3) the key MVT implication (fully proved, taking a derivative bound as hypothesis), (4) Siegel's ineffective bound (axiomized), and (5) the GRH conditional result (axiomized). The Lean insight: `LFunction_apply_one_ne_zero` directly handles nonvanishing; the hard work of effective lower bounds requires Mathlib extensions.
conclusion.implications:
**If no Siegel zeros are proved (i.e., effective Siegel theorem)**:

**For prime distribution**: Linnik's theorem on the smallest prime p ≡ a (mod q) would have an explicit bound p ≤ C·q^L with explicit L. Currently L is known but C is not.

**For cryptography**: Many algorithms use primes in arithmetic progressions; effective lower bounds would give provable efficiency guarantees.

**For Mathlib**: Would require formalizing Landau-Page zeros, zero-free regions of Dirichlet L-functions, and effective Siegel theorem — a major infrastructure investment.

**Connection to GRH**: Siegel zeros are the last obstacle before the full zero-free region program: proving no zeros with Re(s) > 1 - c/log(|Im(s)|+2) would solve many prime distribution problems.
openQuestions: Do Siegel zeros exist? (The central open question — almost certainly NO, but unproved)
Is there an effective version of Siegel's theorem? (Would imply no Siegel zeros with explicit constants)
Can the Landau-Page bound be sharpened? (The 'one exceptional character' — is it really one, or zero?)
What are the implications for Linnik's constant? (Currently known L ≤ 5 for the smallest prime in a progression, but the GRH value would be L = 2)
